SceneOutline: Develop Scene 4 as 3 connected beats, following the story direction.
Outline:
Purpose: Caelen completes his tactical assessment inside the cart, shifting from panic to a cold, transactional mindset as the vehicle approaches its destination.

Viewpoint: Third-person limited (Caelen). He observes the stranger’s posture—relaxed legs crossed, eyes shut—and deduces indifference over malice. The physical sensation of the cart’s suspension confirms the terrain is soft and yielding, suggesting high gravity or deep earth rather than a rough road. His internal monologue reframes his status: he is not a victim of monsters but an inventory item in a ledger that doesn’t yet exist for him. He tests his restraints mentally, noting the raw friction on his broad-palmed wrists and the dulled pain from previous beat trauma.

Objective: To suppress panic and convert fear into hyper-vigilant stillness. Caelen decides resisting movement is futile; he will conserve energy until forced to act again. He categorizes the sounds outside—harsh consonants, rolling vowels—as irrelevant noise, accepting his inability to understand local speech as a temporary hurdle.

Meaningful Change: Caelen’s psychological state transitions from disoriented fear to cold clarity. He accepts his role as "commodity in transit," realizing the captors are merely engaged in a transaction rather than acting out of supernatural evil. This acceptance allows him to stop struggling against ropes and enter a state of passive readiness, preserving stamina for the unknown arrival at the slave pen.

Continuity Dependencies: Relies on approved prose from Scene 3 Beat 2 (capture, collar installation, beating, unconsciousness) and the immediate predecessor beat (cart movement, environmental observation). Maintains the pale yellow sky, heavy gravity sensation, and language barrier established in prior beats. Does not depict arrival at the stone wall or awakening until the next beat.
Prose:
The cart lurched forward, its suspension groaning under the weight of Caelen’s bound body. Every vibration traveled through him like a shockwave, amplified by the unfamiliar density of his new frame. Outside the slats of the cart, the world blurred into streaks of pale yellow. The stone wall he had woken beside slid backward, then vanished entirely, replaced by an endless expanse of hazy horizon and the low, dim sun. There were no mountains, no forests—only a flat, dusty expanse that seemed to stretch forever under the oppressive sky. The terrain was soft, yielding to the wheels, suggesting heavy gravity or simply deep, compacted earth.

Caelen forced himself to stop struggling against the ropes. Resistance only invited more attention, and he had already been beaten into silence once. He lay still, conserving his energy, listening to the creak of the cart’s axle and the distant sound of hooves on gravel. A figure sat opposite him in the cart, legs crossed, eyes closed as if sleeping or ignoring him completely. Caelen watched the man’s profile, noting the calluses on his hands, the practical cut of his tunic, and the lack of any insignia that might indicate rank or faction.

He tried to categorize the sensory input. This wasn’t a dream; there was too much weight here, too much pain. Yet the pain was distant now, dulled by the sheer absurdity of his situation. The air smelled of dust, old leather, and something metallic—blood or rust? He couldn’t tell. His mind struggled to categorize the sounds drifting from outside: harsh consonants and rolling vowels that made no sense in any language he knew.

Caelen looked at the figure opposite him again. No badges, no emblems. Just a man doing a job. The stranger wasn’t looking at him; he was likely checking the horizon or listening for something else entirely. Caelen realized his captors weren’t monsters from a nightmare; they were just people engaged in a transaction. They assessed him as an asset, moved him to a buyer, and nothing more.

He shifted slightly, testing the range of motion allowed by the cord binding his wrists. The friction left raw, stinging trails on his skin. He felt heavy, anchored down by gravity that felt stronger than anything he remembered from Earth. He was inventory. A line item in a ledger that didn’t exist for him yet.

The cart rattled on, carrying him deeper into the alien world, leaving his old life behind in a blur of dust and yellow light. Caelen closed his eyes, not to rest, but to focus. He needed to know how far they had traveled before the sun set, how many hours he had left before another shift or a different pair of hands took charge. He was a prisoner in transit, a commodity being moved from one point of sale to another. The fear that had seized him upon waking had settled into a cold, hard clarity. All he knew was that the ground beneath him was no longer solid earth, but the floor of a cage rolling toward a fate he couldn’t yet name.
